items.title: How can Mississauga residents observe National Day for Truth and Reconciliation?
items.summary: National Day for Truth and Reconciliation is also known as Orange Shirt Day. Mississauga City Hall lit in orange for National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, also known as Orange Shirt Day. In observance of National Day for Truth and Reconciliation on Sept. 30, there are several gatherings and sessions taking place in Mississauga. What: Learn about the importance of Truth and Reconciliation through stories and shared reflection. Attendees are encouraged to wear an orange shirt. Enrolment is in-person the day of, on a first-come, first-served basis. Where: Hazel McCallion Central Library, 301 Burnhamthorpe Rd W. What: Visit the Bradley Museum to learn about the history of Indigenous Peoples in present day Mississauga. Museum staff will share ongoing initiatives to further Reconciliation and the 94 Calls to Action. Tours run every 30 minutes and walk-ins are welcome, though reservations are recommended. Admission is free. What: Flag raising of the Mississaugas of the Credit First Nation flag to recognize the day at Celebration Square and Civic Centre, followed by an evening Clock Tower illumination in orange. Digital screens at the Square will also display the 94 Calls to Action.

items.title: Mississauga mayoral candidate Dipika Damerla spent $31K of taxpayer money on social media: she says it’s a key to democratic engagement
items.summary: A decade ago, it was somewhat simple for taxpayers to call out city council members who mailed out publicly funded flyers and newsletters that functioned as promotional campaign material. Today, when council members spend tens of thousands of dollars of the taxpayers’ money on social media, it’s much harder to tell if the posts are legitimate public information efforts, or little more than a tool to keep the politician’s name in the public eye. One councillor spent more than $31,000 on social media over the current four-year term, while others reported thousands in expenses. The public records reviewed by The Pointer identify the nature of the spending without naming the vendor. Councillors say social media is essential to reaching residents in a city where traditional forms of communication are becoming less effective, particularly among younger residents. As the October 26 municipal election approaches, questions about transparency and accountability inside city hall are tied to many of the biggest issues voters are struggling with. City councillors are always looking for new ways to connect with constituents on these issues, but the way they do this crosses the line when taxpayer-funded communication also serves as an effective self-promotional tool. While residents previously relied on communications from their elected officials through physical hardcopy newsletters delivered to their doorstep, social media has created a new opportunity. Mississauga councillors are increasingly turning to Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, X and other digital platforms to communicate with constituents, but the practice raises concerns about transparency and the use of taxpayer dollars. Trevor Isaac, a resident and vice chair of the umbrella ratepayer group in Mississauga, MIRANET, said residents need more information about how councillors are specifically using social media to communicate with their constituents and how that public money is being used.

items.title: Peel Police Shut Down Westbound Dundas at Tomken After a Pedestrian Is Critically Hurt
items.summary: According to Peel Regional Police, a pedestrian was struck by a vehicle in the area of Dundas Street and Tomken Road in Mississauga and taken to hospital with life-threatening injuries. Police say the collision prompted them to close all westbound lanes on Dundas Street west of Tomken Road while they investigate. No additional details about the victim have been released, according to police. Officers are urging drivers to avoid the area while the road remains closed. Peel police are asking anyone with information about the crash to contact them directly, and tips can also be submitted anonymously through Crime Stoppers, which police say can pay a reward of up to $2,000 for information leading to an arrest.
